Chapter 2. Pooh Goes Visiting and Gets Into a Tight Place 
READ ALOUD


Created by A A Milne in 1924, Winnie the Pooh first appeared in a collection of stories in the London Evening News and later in his own titular book in 1926. He was based on the toy bear by the same name, bought for his son, Christopher Robin. Yes, THAT Christopher Robin, along with Christopher's other stuffed animals, Piglet, Kanga, Roo, Tigger and Eeyore. Owl and Rabbit were later created for the book, and Gopher who appears in the Disney anthology movie, "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh," (1977) was made for the movie - hence his line and play on words, "I'm not in the book!"

'Before writing Winnie-the-Pooh, A. A. Milne was already a successful writer who wrote for the British humor magazine "Punch", had published a mystery novel and was a playwright. Milne began writing poetry for children and later compiled his first verses for publishing, and though his publishers were initially hesitant to publish children's poetry, the poetry collection When We Were Very Young (1924) was a success. It was through this project he met and first collaborated with illustrator E H Shepard.

Among the characters in When We Were Very Young was a teddy bear that Milne modelled after one belonging to his son, Christopher Robin. With the book's success, Shepard encouraged Milne to write stories about Milne's young son  and his stuffed toys, especially the bear he called "Winnie-the-Pooh". Christopher got the name "Winnie" from a bear at the London Zoo, Winnipeg. "Pooh" was the name of a swan they nicknamed while at a stay at the children's hospital.

Milne used Christopher and his toys as inspiration for a series of short stories, which were compiled and published as Winnie-the-Pooh. The model for Pooh remained the bear belonging to Shepard's son. The books of course went on to become a huge success and are now more commonly associated with the Disney franchise.  Penguin Books has called When We Were Very Young, Winnie-the-Pooh, Now We Are Six, and The House At Pooh Corner "the basis of the entire Pooh canon."

On a side note, Winnie the Pooh was HUGE in the late 70's and was everywhere you looked in a Sears & Roebuck, which to translate those last few words to the younger generation, if Amazon was an indoor theme park. But to go on, Winnie the Pooh was huge in my childhood and I had a little doll that had a music box inside that when you wound it, it played the Winnie the Pooh theme. I slept with that doll just about every night until I was six and replaced it with  Gizmo from Gremlins. Signs of the times. All the same, that little yellow bear meant a lot. 

It was a marker of my childhood, and a memory that reminded me, 'whatever happens to us on the way, in that enchanted place on the top of the Forest, a little child and their Bear will always be playing.'

check out "When We Were Very Young", "Now We Are Six", and "The House At Pooh Corner" by A. A. Milne
